lesson.title: From Evil Empire to Negotiating Table: The Cold War Winds Down
lesson.summary: Reagan entered office determined to confront the Soviet Union as an evil empire and rebuild American military strength, but by the end of the decade he was meeting regularly with a new Soviet leader, and the Cold War was winding toward its end.
lesson.body:
Reagan came into office in 1981 committed to reversing what he saw as a decade of American weakness relative to the Soviet Union, and his administration pursued the largest peacetime military buildup in American history, funded in part through the tax and spending choices at the heart of Reaganomics. In a March 1983 speech to the National Association of Evangelicals, Reagan famously called the Soviet Union an evil empire, language that broke sharply with the more cautious tone of detente era diplomacy from the 1970s. That same month he announced the Strategic Defense Initiative, nicknamed Star Wars by critics and the press, a proposed missile defense system meant to shield the United States from nuclear attack, which alarmed Soviet leaders who feared it could upset the strategic balance the two superpowers had maintained through mutual vulnerability.

The arms race that had defined the Cold War for decades took on new intensity in the early 1980s, with both superpowers deploying new generations of nuclear missiles in Europe and elsewhere, and tensions rising to levels not seen since the Cuban Missile Crisis. Yet the same arms race that Reagan pushed to new heights also set the stage for a dramatic turn toward negotiation, once a new kind of Soviet leader emerged.

That leader was Mikhail Gorbachev, who came to power in the Soviet Union in 1985. Reagan and Gorbachev met at a series of summits that transformed the relationship between the two countries: in Geneva in 1985, in Reykjavik, Iceland in 1986, where the two leaders came surprisingly close to an agreement to eliminate nuclear weapons entirely, and in Washington in December 1987, where they signed the Intermediate Range Nuclear Forces Treaty, the first agreement to eliminate an entire class of nuclear weapons. At a 1988 summit in Moscow, Reagan was asked whether he still considered the Soviet Union an evil empire, and he said that description belonged to another time, a remarkable shift from his rhetoric just five years earlier.

By the time Reagan left office in January 1989, the foundation for the Cold War's end had been laid, though the dramatic events that actually brought it to a close, the collapse of Soviet control over Eastern Europe and the dissolution of the Soviet Union itself, unfolded under his successor, George H.W. Bush, between 1989 and 1991. Bush and Gorbachev declared the Cold War over at a summit off the coast of Malta in December 1989, closing a chapter of confrontation and negotiation that had run from Reagan's early hardline rhetoric to a genuinely transformed relationship between Washington and Moscow.
